title: Wenceslaus (28 September)
hook: the good king of the carol was a duke, and his own brother had him killed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cosmas and Damian, the brothers who healed without a bill. Your line was the free doctors. What did you give away without charging? Day one thousand twenty-nine.

Snow, deep and crisp and even. A king looks out his window on the feast of Stephen, sees a poor man gathering firewood, and sets off through the storm with food and wine, his page stepping in his footprints to keep from freezing. That's the Christmas carol. It's an English Victorian song, written long after the man it names. The real Wenceslaus was not a king, and his story doesn't end at a warm table. It ends at a church door. Today, Wenceslaus.
screen: `A KING IN THE SNOW.` → `A CAROL WRITTEN LONG AFTER.` → `A STORY THAT ENDS AT A CHURCH DOOR.`

segments.voice: Wenceslaus, Václav in Czech, was a duke of Bohemia, in the lands that are now the Czech Republic. Tradition remembers him as a ruler who prayed, helped the poor, and tried to govern as a Christian when the court around him was split over the faith. His grandmother Ludmila, also honored as a saint, raised him in it. Not everyone in the family was pleased. His younger brother, Boleslaus, wanted power. The old accounts tell it this way: Boleslaus invited Wenceslaus to a feast. The next morning, as Wenceslaus walked to Mass, his brother and his men attacked him at the door of the church, and he died there. Brother against brother, at the doorway to worship. It's a story as old as Genesis. In Genesis, after Cain kills Abel, God asks him where his brother is, and Cain answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Am I my brother's keeper?" In the Wenceslaus story, that old question comes back at a church door. In time, people began to honor Wenceslaus as a martyr, and he became the patron of the Czech people. In Prague, a great square bears his name, with his statue on horseback at the top. The carol calls him a king anyway: good king Wenceslas. Not a title he held. In the song, a title he earned.
screen: `A DUKE OF BOHEMIA, NOT A KING.` · `HIS BROTHER WANTED POWER.` · `KILLED AT THE CHURCH DOOR.` · `A TITLE HE EARNED, NOT HELD.` · then, large: `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a divided family. Let your shoulders drop and breathe. Bring to mind a family that's split, yours or someone else's: siblings who don't speak, parents and children who can't be in the same room. Don't fix it. Just hold both sides, without choosing a winner. If you pray, you can name them before God, and ask for one small thaw. If you don't, simply wish them, each of them, a little peace. The bell holds the time.
Wenceslaus. A duke of Bohemia who governed as a Christian, was killed by his brother's men at a church door, and is remembered in a carol as the good king.
Your line: good king. Today, do what the king in the carol does: bring something warm to someone out in the cold. A meal, a coat, a ride, a visit. Day one thousand twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Saint Wenceslaus is remembered on 28 September, a national feast in the Czech Republic; Catholics there keep it with Mass, and his statue in Prague's Wenceslas Square is a gathering place.

notes: Hook paraphrases images from J. M. Neale's carol ('deep and crisp and even', feast of Stephen, the page in his footprints); the carol is public domain but not on the validator's translation list, so it is cited unquoted. Confirm.
Killed by his brother's men at the church door on the way to Mass: the old legends vary on details (Boleslaus striking first, the companions finishing it); confirm the summary.
'He would not raise a hand against his brother': based on the legends' account; confirm or soften.
'A story as old as Genesis' refers to Cain and Abel; confirm tone.
Trapdoor: confirm that the earliest lives are Latin and Old Church Slavonic, and that the carol is Victorian.
Fork setup says only 'bad blood over who should rule'; the legends do not say he knew of the plot.
Spelling: the calendar form is Wenceslaus; the carol and the Prague square use Wenceslas.

Editor: cut 'the old lives say he would not raise a hand against his brother' (some legends have him overpower Boleslaus first); cut the guess about why the carol made him a king; the carry no longer repeats day 1017's 'use your little say' angle and now follows the carol's errand (day 1030's review updated to match).
